# Linh's Story

Linh was twenty-two when it happened. She had been married to Marcus for just over a year—a quiet, steady man who worked in IT and had always been gentle with her. They lived in a small apartment in suburban Virginia, and she had taken a job at a call center processing insurance claims, the kind of work that paid enough and left her evenings free. The assault came on a Tuesday night in March when she stayed late to finish a stack of files. The building was nearly empty. A supervisor she barely knew—a man named Derek who had always made her uncomfortable with his lingering eye contact—had followed her into the parking garage. What happened there lasted perhaps ten minutes but fractured something in Linh that would not come back together.

The first weeks after were a blur of numbness and practical necessity. She told Marcus it had been someone she didn't know, that she had fought back, that she was fine. She wasn't fine. By the time she returned to work a month later, Linh had begun to notice that certain moments would send her spiraling. The sound of sirens made her stomach clench—the ambulance that had come that night was still vivid in her mind, its wail somehow tied to the moment she realized what was happening. When her mother called to talk about her cousin's wedding, full of excitement about the happy family gathering, Linh felt a sharp, inexplicable panic, as though joy itself had become dangerous. Stress at work, the pressure of a difficult call or a missed deadline, would trigger an immediate sense of threat, and with it, fragmented sensory memories she couldn't quite assemble: the smell of the garage, the taste of blood in her mouth from where she had bitten her cheek, the rough texture of concrete against her skin. When these triggers surfaced—a colleague's mention of Derek, the sound of a door slamming in the office—Linh had learned to leave immediately, stepping outside or retreating to the bathroom until her heart rate settled. She had begun timing her breaks to avoid the break room when certain people were there, and she stopped taking the direct route through the parking garage to her car, adding twenty minutes to her commute rather than risk the memories that place could unleash. These memories didn't come like normal recollections—they felt more real than the present moment, more vivid and insistent than what was actually happening around her. When the fragmented sensory details surfaced unbidden—the smell, the taste, the texture—Linh would find herself reaching for distraction, scrolling through her phone for sexual content, or initiating sexual activity with Marcus as a way to override the intrusive images with a different kind of sensation, something she could control.

What frightened Linh most was the thought that if she allowed herself to think about the event directly, to sit with it and try to understand it, she would shatter. This conviction had taken root quickly and felt absolutely true. She had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, that the world contained threats she had to scan for constantly. Because she was certain that her mind would fracture if she truly examined what had happened, she found herself turning away from anything that might force that confrontation—she stopped journaling, avoided therapy homework, and when Marcus gently suggested she talk to someone, she resisted, convinced that speaking about it would only make the conviction real. Her belief that she was fundamentally inadequate also drove her to seek control in the one place it felt available: she channeled the tension and shame into sexual activity, a way to reclaim agency over her body that felt safer than the vulnerability of being truly seen. The moment she entered a room—the call center break room, a grocery store, anywhere—her eyes would move immediately to the exits, cataloging them, calculating routes. Her body had become a surveillance system. She flinched at unexpected movement, her nervous system interpreting a colleague's sudden gesture or a door slamming as a sign of imminent danger. The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller—she began calling in sick on days when the parking garage felt too exposed, she stopped attending team meetings in person, and she found herself checking the locks on her apartment door twice before bed, a ritual that had become the only way her body would settle enough to sleep. And beneath it all ran a deeper conviction: she was inadequate, fundamentally broken in some way that had made her vulnerable to this.

The maladaptive strategies had developed almost without her noticing. When stress triggered the fragmented memories and the certainty that she couldn't handle them, Linh would turn to sexual fantasies and activities—a way to channel the tension and reclaim some sense of control over her body. When reminders of the event surfaced, usually through a colleague mentioning something that brought Derek's face to mind, she would find herself reaching for her phone, seeking distraction through sexual content. And authority figures—anyone in uniform, anyone with power over her—had become intolerable. She had requested a transfer away from the supervisor team and now worked under a manager she barely knew, which meant she was constantly tense in her own workplace, scanning for the moment someone in a position of power might approach her. Marcus had noticed her withdrawal, the way she seemed distant during intimate moments, the way her body would sometimes go rigid without explanation. He didn't understand, and she couldn't explain it to him without reliving it.

The cycle had tightened over the past six months. Each time a trigger surfaced—stress at work, the sight of an ambulance in traffic, her mother's cheerful talk of family gatherings—it would activate the vivid, fragmented memories, which in turn would confirm her belief that she couldn't handle her own mind, that she needed to be hypervigilant, that she was fundamentally inadequate. The sexual coping would provide temporary relief, but it also became its own trigger, leaving her feeling ashamed and more convinced of her inadequacy. Her scanning for danger and exits had become so automatic that she was exhausted by it; her startle response had made her colleagues nervous around her. She had called in sick twice last week, unable to face the call center, unable to face Marcus, unable to face the idea that this might be her life now.

It was Marcus who finally insisted she see someone. He had found her at three in the morning, curled on the bathroom floor, unable to articulate why she was there. Linh had agreed, not because she believed it would help, but because she was terrified. What frightened her most was not the memories themselves, but the conviction that acknowledging them would mean she truly was broken—that there was no coming back from this.

Fragmented memories activate threat and reinforce appraisals, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that the memories themselves drive the maladaptive strategies; the sexual coping is presented as a response to stress and tension, not directly to the memory.

REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: Triggers activate memories and threat responses, but no paragraph conveys that triggers directly drive maladaptive strategies; the connection is only indirect through memory and threat.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: Negative appraisals (inadequacy, conviction she cannot handle her mind) are present, but no paragraph shows them directly causing maladaptive strategies; the sexual coping appears to be driven by stress and fragmented memories rather than by the appraisals themselves.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: Fragmented memories activate threat and reinforce appraisals, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that the memories themselves drive the maladaptive strategies; the sexual coping is presented as a response to stress and tension, not directly to the memory.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: Threat perception (hypervigilance, scanning for danger) is prominent, but no paragraph shows threat directly causing maladaptive strategies; the sexual coping is presented as a response to stress and fragmented memories, not as a consequence of the threat response itself.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
